title: Where does a battery get its energy?
answer: A battery contains materials that can react with each other. You can connect the two ends into a circuit so the reaction helps move electrons around the outside path. Inside the battery, other charged particles move through a material called an electrolyte. Together, the two movements let it supply electrical energy. A battery can only keep doing this while enough of its stored chemical energy remains. Recharging some batteries changes the materials back toward their earlier state.
facts: The ends of many batteries are marked with plus and minus signs.

title: What happens when lights share one path?
answer: In a series circuit, the electric current has one path to follow. Imagine a wire from a small battery to a lamp, then to another lamp, then back to the battery. Current runs through both lamps in turn. If one connection opens, it breaks the only path and both lamps go out. A switch put anywhere along that path can turn both lamps off together. A lamp needs a closed path before it can shine.
facts: The same amount of current flows through each part of a single series path.

title: How can two lights work separately on one battery?
answer: Imagine two lamps connected so each has its own path between the battery’s ends. Electricity can travel in both branches of this parallel circuit. If one branch is opened by a switch, the other still has a complete path, so its lamp can stay lit. Most homes use the same general idea for many devices. Turning off your bedroom lamp need not stop the light across the hallway. A circuit can also use both series and parallel ideas in different places.
facts: Branches connected between the same pair of points have the same voltage across them.

title: Why can a rubbed balloon stick to a wall?
answer: Rub a balloon against some fabrics and a few electrons can move from one surface to the other. That leaves one surface with extra negative charge and the other with less. Bringing the balloon close to a wall can shift charges in the wall slightly. The opposite charges are then a little closer to the balloon than the similar charges are. The pull of the closer charges can be strong enough to hold the balloon up for a while.
facts: “Static” describes charge that has collected on a surface instead of flowing steadily in a circuit.

title: How an electromagnet turns magnetism on and off
answer: When current runs through a wire, it makes a magnetic field around it. Winding the wire into a coil lets the fields of many loops work together. A piece of iron inside the coil can make that effect stronger. Some cranes use a large electromagnet to lift a load containing iron or steel. They can stop its electric current to let the load go. Electric motors and other machines use coils in different ways to make controlled movement.
facts: Magnetism made by the coil depends on current flowing in the wire.

title: Why electricity changes voltage along the way
answer: A transformer normally has two coils of wire arranged around a shared piece of magnetic material. Current changing direction in the first coil makes its magnetic field change too. That changing field makes a voltage across the second coil. The number of loops in each coil helps set how much the voltage changes. Power companies use higher voltages for carrying power far along wires and then reduce it near the places that need to use the electricity.
facts: A simple transformer needs a changing current to keep producing an effect in the second coil.

title: Why some electrical problems turn the power off
answer: A wire can heat up if more electric current passes through it than it was made to carry. A protective device called a circuit breaker can open the wire’s path automatically. Current then stops flowing along that path, cutting power to the parts it supplies. A fuse serves a similar purpose but uses a small piece of metal that melts to break the path. In either case, opening the circuit helps keep the wiring from overheating.
facts: A circuit breaker and a light switch both open a circuit, but the breaker can do it automatically when there is a problem.

title: How a tiny LED makes light
answer: An LED is a small electronic part made from special solid materials. When electric current goes through it in the intended direction, charges inside can give some of their energy away as light. Different materials can produce different colors. A white LED lamp can use a coating that changes some of the light’s color so the mix looks white. Light from an LED does not depend on heating a wire until it glows.
facts: An LED still warms up a bit, even though much of the useful energy can come out as visible light.

title: Why electric toaster wires glow
answer: Inside a toaster, electric current travels through narrow heating elements. The elements resist the motion of charge, so some of the electrical energy becomes warmth in the metal. They can get hot enough to give off light and send heat toward both sides of the bread. As the outside of the bread warms, it becomes drier and browns. In a pop-up toaster, a spring can lift the bread when the heating time is over.

facts: The first electric toasters often toasted only one side at a time.

title: How a stovetop can heat the pan directly
answer: Under the surface of an induction cooktop is a coil of wire. A changing current in the coil makes a changing magnetic field. In a suitable metal pan above it, that changing field can produce currents in the metal. The pan’s resistance turns some of the energy into heat inside the pan. It then warms food by touching it. The cooktop’s top can still become hot because the hot pan rests on it.
facts: An induction cooktop depends on both the changing magnetic field and a pan made with suitable material.

title: How a capacitor holds a burst of energy
answer: A capacitor can hold energy by keeping opposite charges apart. Many capacitors have two pieces of metal separated by a very thin layer that does not let charge pass easily. An electric circuit can move charge so one side has more electrons and the other has fewer. If a circuit later gives the charges a path to come back together, the capacitor can supply energy for a short time. Some camera flashes use this quick release.
facts: A capacitor and a battery both store energy, but a capacitor need not use the same sort of chemical reaction.

title: How quartz helps a clock count seconds
answer: A quartz clock contains a little piece of a mineral that can vibrate. An electronic circuit gives the quartz small pushes so it vibrates at a regular rate. The clock counts those vibrations and turns each set into a step of time. That step can update a display or tell a tiny motor to move hands. Older mechanical clocks can count swings of a much bigger part. The quartz clock uses a much smaller movement.
facts: A common watch crystal vibrates more than thirty thousand times in one second.

title: Why airplanes change the shape of their wings
answer: If you look out at a plane’s wing near landing, parts along the back may slide out or tilt down. These parts are called flaps. They change the size or shape of the wing so it can make more lift while moving more slowly. Flaps can also add drag, which helps a plane slow down. On flights that are cruising quickly, the flaps usually move back into the wing so the air can flow past more easily.
aliases: why do wings change before landing
facts: Some wings also have movable parts on the front edge that help with slow flight.

title: How do airplane wings and tails steer?
answer: An airplane can point its nose up or down, turn it left or right, or tip one wing lower than the other. Moving parts push on flowing air to help make these turns. A pair of parts near the wing tips, called ailerons, help tip the airplane. A small moving surface on the tail helps raise or lower the nose. The rudder on the upright part of the tail helps swing the nose from side to side.
facts: Tipping a wing, lifting the nose and swinging the nose are called roll, pitch and yaw.

title: Why airports have traffic control towers
answer: Many airports have tall towers where controllers can look out at the runways and paths between gates. They talk with pilots and help keep aircraft apart while airplanes land, take off or move on the ground. Other controllers watch displays and coordinate flights farther from an airport. Bad weather may mean only a few planes can use a runway at once. In that case, the controllers and the people planning traffic can change when planes arrive.
aliases: what do air traffic controllers do
facts: Keeping aircraft apart is one of the controller’s most important jobs.

title: What do the big numbers at the end of a runway mean?
answer: A runway is a strip where an aircraft can take off and land. Large numbers at the ends usually describe the direction a plane faces as it goes along the strip. In the United States, the numbers usually come from the direction measured with a magnetic compass, rounded and shortened. The other end points nearly the opposite way. White lines down the middle can mark the center, and other markings can show where a landing area begins.
aliases: why do runways have white markings
facts: At airports with several parallel runways, letters sometimes tell apart strips that have nearly the same direction.

title: How a traffic light can detect a waiting car
answer: Some traffic lights follow a schedule, while others can change when a vehicle is waiting. One kind of detector uses wire arranged in a loop under the road. Electricity in the loop produces a magnetic field, and a large metal vehicle above it changes the electrical behavior a little. The detector sends a message to the traffic signal’s controller. A signal can also detect vehicles using a camera or equipment that sends radio waves.
aliases: how traffic lights know cars are waiting
facts: A detector can tell a signal that a car is in a lane without needing to know who is driving.

title: Why build a circle where roads meet?
answer: A modern roundabout sends traffic around a small island so paths join in the same direction. The road bends as it leads toward the center, which helps drivers slow before entering the circle. Drivers can then move off along the road they need. Where an ordinary crossing allows several paths to cut across one another, a roundabout has fewer places where moving vehicles meet at right angles. The island’s shape helps guide cars, buses and trucks along useful paths.
facts: A roundabout is shaped to make drivers travel more slowly where paths join.

title: Where does rain on a street go?
answer: After rain falls on a street, much of it cannot soak through the hard surface. Water runs along slopes and gutters to an opening or grate. Some drains send this water through pipes to a pond, stream or river. The rain can carry soil, trash or oil it picked up along the way. Unlike the water that leaves a sink, stormwater in many places goes through different pipes. Some older systems share pipes for both.
facts: Moving rainwater from hard surfaces is called runoff.

title: Why some gardens are planted lower than the ground
answer: A rain garden looks like a shallow hollow planted with things that can handle occasional wet soil. Water rushing off a roof, road or path can spread out and slow down in the hollow. The slower water has more time to soak through the soil, where some loose bits and other materials can be removed. After the garden drains, the plants can keep growing. Rain gardens can reduce the stream of water reaching a storm drain.
facts: A rain garden holds water for a short time, rather than staying full all year.

title: How railway signals help keep trains apart
answer: One way to manage a railway is to divide it into sections called blocks. Equipment can tell a signaling system whether a train is in a block. Signals then help the next driver or automatic controls know whether the route ahead is available. This matters because a heavy train needs a long distance to stop, so relying only on seeing another train could leave too little time. Railways use several ways to detect trains and share information.

facts: Some signal systems use equipment in the tracks to tell whether a train is present.

title: How can a printer build an object you can pick up?
answer: A 3D printer can turn a computer model into a solid object. Its program pictures the model as many very thin horizontal layers. One type of printer pushes out soft plastic to draw each layer. As the plastic cools or hardens, the next layer can join to it. Other printers build layers from powder or liquid. The object grows layer by layer, unlike a part made by carving away the material around its outline.
facts: Making a shape by adding layers is called additive manufacturing.

title: How a door knows someone is coming
answer: An automatic door often uses a sensor to look for movement near the entrance. Some sensors send out radio waves and notice a change when those waves bounce off a moving person. A controller then tells a motor to slide the door open. A second kind of sensing can look for someone still in the doorway, so movement alone does not decide whether it closes. The motor moves the door back when the opening is clear.
facts: Sensors can have separate jobs when they detect movement and when they look for a person remaining in a space.

title: What do the stripes on a barcode say?
answer: A striped barcode uses dark bars and light gaps of different widths to represent numbers. A scanner can shine light on the stripes and measure the pattern that comes back. The equipment turns that pattern into a number with a known meaning. At a store, the number often identifies the type and size of product so a computer can look up its name or its price. Bottles of the same kind can share the same number.
facts: A store’s own computer normally looks up the price. The stripes do not need to spell out a dollar amount.
